Classical Energies Learn to Reason 1,000×\times Faster than Looped Models

Benjamin Hoover1    Hugh Blayney1    James C. R. Whittington1
Abstract

Looped models have emerged as a prominent paradigm for reasoning, with successes on simple reasoning puzzles such as Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique. However, these models can be unstable, slow to train, and use many parameters and FLOPs to solve simple puzzles. Descent on an energy not only mitigates these issues but also offers advantages: built-in early stopping, compute that adapts to problem difficulty, fast training without differentiating through a solver, and interpretable weights that learn the constraints of the puzzle. Here we demonstrate this with a learned version of Hopfield & Tank’s energy from the 80s, which we term CRAM, solves 99.996% of Sudoku-Extreme and 100% of Maze-Unique test puzzles after 42 ms and 132 ms of training on one GPU, at least 1,000×{\times} faster than looped models on these tasks. CRAM also matches baseline looped models at their highest accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme using at least 282×{\times} fewer inference FLOPs. Our work suggests two things. First, that energies are an extremely promising direction for training reasoning from data. Second, a caution against using trivially solvable benchmarks like Sudoku and Maze to test the scalability of looped reasoning techniques.

††footnotetext: 1Prefrontal, London, United Kingdom. Correspondence to Benjamin Hoover <ben@prefrontal.ai>, James C.R. Whittington <james@prefrontal.ai>

1 Introduction

An emerging new paradigm for reasoning is looping, in which a layer, or block of layers, is repeatedly applied to produce an answer. Small looped models [62, 38] (millions of parameters) have had successes on simple benchmarks such as Sudoku and mazes. However, they are slow to train in part due to their use of truncated backprop-through-time (BPTT), and the reasons behind their successes remain unclear [2, 51].

Energy minimization is a related framework that offers a principled approach to looping. Here, each loop step corresponds to a gradient descent step on an energy function. Minimizing energy offers many potential benefits, such as guaranteed stability, early stopping, and efficient training methods that bypass the need for BPTT. Indeed, looped reasoners have begun adopting the ideas of energy-based networks without adopting an explicit energy. Some train their updates to converge to attractors or fixed points, a guarantee intrinsic to energy network dynamics [36, 44]. Others learn when to stop with a separate halting network [28, 5, 62, 38]. Each of these desirable properties is generally added on top of the looped network through an extra head, loss, or module, and the network is trained by backpropagating through its repeated applications. With looped models rebuilding the desirable properties of an energy one at a time, we ask: why not learn the energy directly?

It’s already known that constraint puzzles like Sudoku have a corresponding energy that, when minimized, solves the puzzle [34]. In the 1980’s, Hopfield and Tank showed how to hand-design an energy function that solves certain classes of logic problems [35]. It is, however, less well understood if an explicit energy can be learned from data to solve a wide array of reasoning problems.

Here, we develop a trainable version of the Hopfield-Tank energy and then learn the weights directly from puzzles. We call this tiny trainable energy, together with the recurrent dynamics that descend it at inference time, a Compact Reasoning Associative Memory (CRAM).We call it this because, as in a Hopfield network [32], its weights memorize associations between pairs of valid cells, and descent on the energy completes a corrupted pattern (i.e., a puzzle provided with only its clues). CRAM’s energy is a special case of the energies of modern Hopfield networks [40, 41].

In this work we: 1) show that CRAM trains at least 1,000×{\times} faster than modern looped models and reasons with at least 282×{\times} fewer inference FLOPs on a variety of different puzzles (Sudoku-Extreme [62], Maze-Unique [36], and the N-Queens and graph-coloring sets of Baek et al. [3]); 2) show that CRAM provides a stopping test that allows compute to scale with the difficulty of a puzzle; 3) show that CRAM is data-efficient, learning interpretable weights from Sudoku-Extreme using an order of magnitude fewer training puzzles than looped models; 4) show that local training objectives train fastest compared to other methods of training the same energy — significantly faster than BPTT; and 5) show that a hand-set CRAM energy with few unique weights can solve every test puzzle from every benchmark exactly.

CRAM represents the state of the art on speed and efficiency of looping to solve constraint puzzles, by several orders of magnitude. However, since these puzzles can be solved easily with so few parameters using CRAM, our work suggests that high accuracy on these benchmarks are not indicative of future performance on harder tasks. Indeed, CRAM’s simple energy on its own would struggle to learn more complex reasoning tasks like ARC-AGI [12], though we do show how a simple latent extension of CRAM can solve Maze-Hard near perfectly in App. F. Nevertheless, the dramatic speed-up that this energy provides on the presented tasks offers a potential path forward for data-efficient general reasoning capabilities.

2 Background

CRAM’s energy is a form of pairwise graphical model in that it is a sum of costs on and between cells, as in the energy of a Markov random field (MRF) [7, 61]. Learning these costs goes by several names, such as constraint programming [54] or constraint acquisition [9, 6, 15]. Recent methods show that you can learn pairwise costs for Sudoku directly from solved puzzles, using approximate likelihood methods like those studied in this work [10, 16, 17]. However, to infer solutions to new puzzles, these methods pass the learned constraints to an external solver [13]. CRAM keeps this learning problem but uses neural optimization methods to replace the external solver with recurrent search on its own energy [35, 47].

Energy-based networks treat an energy over a large search space of possible solutions as the objective of both training and inference. Training shapes the energy to be low at observed data; inference or “reasoning” minimizes the energy to sample low-energy solutions (see Fig. 1) [32, 42]. Hopfield and Tank used a version of the Hopfield Network with continuous neurons to solve constraint problems like the Traveling Salesman Problem with hand-set weights [33, 35], and later work did the same for Sudoku [34]. CRAM writes these energies in a mean-field free energy form with learnable weights [47]. This form approximates the free energy of a Boltzmann machine, which have similarly been applied to logic and combinatorial problems [1, 30, 14, 59]. However, none of these energies have been trained by observing puzzle solutions alone.

Modern looped reasoners use deep, weight-tied networks to learn puzzles directly from data. HRM and TRM popularized this design for Sudoku, mazes and ARC, building on recurrent relational networks and universal transformers [62, 38, 12, 46, 18]. Later works varied the architecture but kept the same training approach: backpropagating through the reasoning trajectory of a depth-recurrent model to refine the model’s prediction for a specified input [25, 3, 55, 24, 64, 39, 57, 52]. Some approaches use diffusion- and flow-style training to avoid BPTT [21, 64, 39, 29, 65, 57]. Others engineer fixed point behavior into deep models, training the update loop to converge to stable equilibria [36, 44, 29, 65, 23]. This last direction holds promise, since Hopfield & Tank already showed that these reasoning puzzles are naturally suited to fixed-point problems.

Energy-based looped models encourage convergence by training an energy on top of a deep network, seeking to combine the best of looped models with advantages of Hopfield Networks and Boltzmann Machines [20, 21, 27, 43, 49, 66, 11]. For example, concurrent work Energy-Based Reasoners (EBR) [11] showcases several advantages of energy for looped model reasoning: it trains an energy on the latent states of a TRM-style transformer, descends it with noisy projected gradient steps, and stops when the gradient norm is small [11]. Though similar in spirit, these networks are much larger and slower than CRAM, and all of them learn through BPTT.

3 Method

The reasoning tasks studied in this work can be represented via MM answer variables called cells, each with up to CC candidate values. Therefore, an energy is assigned to each M×CM\times C belief array 𝒑{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}, whose (non-negative) entry pi​a{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}p}_{ia} gives the probability of candidate value aa at cell ii. Simply, 𝒑i{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{i} is modeled as a softmax distribution over possible answers for cell ii.

with learnable parameters 𝜽\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}} and inverse temperature β>0\beta>0. For each pair of cells i,ji,j, the matrix 𝑲i​j∈ℝC×C\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}K}}_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times C} contains trainable “costs” for all pairs of candidate values. The vector 𝑩i∈ℝC\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}B}}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} is a “bias” that describes the cost of each belief at cell ii. When 𝒑i{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{i} is one-hot, the entropy term is zero, and Eq. 1 is simply the sum of the pair and input costs of the chosen values. This energy is a mean-field free energy, which extends the energy of a continuous Hopfield network to CC-state neurons [47, 33].

Reasoning as energy minimization.

CRAM infers solutions by recurrently minimizing the energy of Eq. 1 with a puzzle’s givens held fixed; this is termed relaxation. Each cell has an unconstrained recurrent neuron state 𝒗i∈ℝC{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} which is used as the logits for the belief 𝒑i=softmax⁡(β​𝒗i){\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{i}=\operatorname{softmax}(\beta{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i}) over possible answer states. With time constant τi>0\tau_{i}>0, free neuron states evolve as the derivative of the energy,

We are able to update 𝒗i{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i} using the gradient of EE w.r.t. 𝒑i{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{i} because the softmax is a monotonic function, so convergence to the same fixed 𝒑i⋆{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{i}^{\star} is still guaranteed. With equal time constants τ\tau and step size η=Δ​t/τ\eta=\Delta t/\tau, an Euler step of Eq. 2 is:

𝒗i←(1−η)​𝒗i−η⁡(∑j𝑾i​j​𝒑j+𝑩i).{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i}\leftarrow(1-\eta){\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i}-\eta\Big(\sum_{j}\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}W}}_{ij}{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{j}+\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}B}}_{i}\Big). (3)

With η=1\eta=1, this is the one-step update 𝒗i←−∑j𝑾i​j𝒑j−𝑩i{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i}\leftarrow-\sum_{j}\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}W}}_{ij}{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{j}-\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}B}}_{i}, so each iteration is one layer of recurrence, as in looped models. For fixed parameters and temperature, the deterministic descent of Eq. 2 guarantees that the energy never increases in continuous time (i.e., d​E/d​t≤0dE/dt\leq 0, see App. E). We find that randomness during inference is important to help escape local minima and explore distinct solutions, so for our experiments we use a form of Gibbs sampling known as focused Gibbs search which prioritizes cell updates based on their local energy [35, 26]. The energy also provides a natural early-stopping criterion: search can stop either when a board’s energy is at most a threshold fitted from the training solutions, or when no single-cell change lowers the energy (App. C).

Training shapes the energy.

A common principle of energy-based learning is to lower the energy of observed solutions 𝒙∼Pdata{\color[rgb]{0.0938,0.6406,0.4453}\boldsymbol{x}}\sim P_{\mathrm{data}}, and raise that of competing answers or negative samples 𝒙−∼P𝜽{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{x}}^{-}\sim P_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}} favored by the model, where P𝜽​(𝒙−)∝exp⁡[−E𝜽​(𝒙−)]P_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{x}}^{-})\propto\exp[-E_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{x}}^{-})] is the Boltzmann distribution induced by the model’s energy [1, 42]. This objective is depicted in Fig. 1 and mathematically described as

∇𝜽𝒥ML​(𝜽)=𝔼𝒙∼Pdata​[∇𝜽E𝜽​(𝒙)]⏟lower energy on data−𝔼𝒙−∼P𝜽​[∇𝜽E𝜽​(𝒙−)]⏟raise energy on model samples.\nabla_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{ML}}(\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}})=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0938,0.6406,0.4453}\boldsymbol{x}}\sim P_{\mathrm{data}}}\!\left[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}E_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}({\color[rgb]{0.0938,0.6406,0.4453}\boldsymbol{x}})\right]}_{\mathclap{\text{\scriptsize lower energy on data}}}-\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{x}}^{-}\sim P_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}}\!\left[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}E_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{x}}^{-})\right]}_{\mathclap{\text{\scriptsize raise energy on model samples}}}. (4)

Throughout, green identifies training labels.

Importantly, these methods avoid differentiating through relaxation (i.e., the looping of Eq. 3). This can significantly reduce fitting cost compared to BPTT, which must propagate gradients through a reasoning trajectory.

Raising energy on model samples (the second term of Eq. 4) can be prohibitively expensive, and several methods approximate it with samples from short Markov chains or relaxations [31, 58, 45]. In this paper, we primarily use a pseudolikelihood (PL) objective for its combination of high accuracy, simplicity, and short fitting time on these tasks [8, 37], though other methods are similarly effective (see Table 7). See Secs. D.1 and C for training details.

4 Experiments

In our experiments, a learned energy loses no accuracy against looped models, trains at least 1,000×{\times} faster, and uses less inference compute (Sec. 4.1). Its stopping test lets compute follow the difficulty of a puzzle, and its learned weights can be read as the rules of a puzzle (Sec. 4.2). It trains fastest with local objectives, and from few training puzzles (Sec. 4.3). Finally, we show that simple CRAM energies whose weights are set by hand from the rules of each task solves all tested benchmarks at least as accurately as every trained baseline, using at most three unique weights (Sec. 4.3).

Tasks.

We evaluate CRAM on four reasoning tasks: Sudoku-Extreme [62] (a set of hard 9×99\times 9 Sudoku puzzles), Maze-Unique [36] (a set of 30×3030\times 30 mazes whose answer is the unique path between two endpoints), N-Queens, and Graph Coloring [3, 11] (tasks that have many valid answers per input). Every task trains the pairwise energy of Eq. 1, and we specify how each task informs the structure of CRAM’s weights in Table 1. In no task is the energy told the rules of a puzzle.

Baselines.

We test against HRM [62], Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) [38], Generative Recursive Reasoning (GRAM) [3], Equilibrium Reasoners (EqR) [36], Flow Reasoning Models (FRM) [29], Tiny Recursive Message Passing (TRMP) [52] and Energy Based Reasoners (EBR) [11]. Where available, we retrain each baseline with its authors’ code and recipe on one H200 for timing and score each baseline with its published inference setting.11 1 The training code of TRMP is not released, so we reimplement TRMP from the recipe in its paper (Sec. C.8). We score every method on the same test set of each task, and no method chooses a setting or a checkpoint on the test set (Sec. C.1). CRAM and each baseline trains with three seeds, and we report the mean over the three runs. We compare only against models that produce the answer by their own recurrent computation. Methods that pass learned costs to an external exact solver [10, 16, 17] are outside the scope of this work.

Training CRAM.

CRAM weights are initialized to zero and are trained to minimizes the PL objective of Eq. 5 at the labeled solutions using with SGD with momentum and a cosine schedule. The priors of Table 1 enter as shared weights or, on Sudoku-Extreme, as digit relabeling of the training boards. We take the final trained model and do not select a best performing checkpoint when reporting CRAM’s results (App. C). Training runs finish by computing the stopping threshold from the training solutions (their highest energy plus a small tolerance); reported fit times include this step.

4.1 Comparison with looped models

High accuracy at small sizes and fast training.

Does a CRAM energy that learns from solved puzzles reach the accuracy of looped models, and at what cost? Table 2 compares CRAM with the seven looped baselines on Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique. On both tasks, CRAM is the most accurate method, solving 99.996% of the Sudoku-Extreme test puzzles and every Maze-Unique test maze. The most accurate looped model, TRMP, solves 99.87% and 99.23%. CRAM reaches this accuracy with thousands of times less training time than every looped model. All results are trained from examples except the gray rows of Table 2, which are a reference for an optimal CRAM energy that is coded by hand from the puzzles explicit constraints (Sec. 4.3).

Efficient inference.

Each method has a setting that allows us to vary its maximum allowed inference budget: the number of reasoning steps (HRM, TRM, FRM), restarts (EqR), sampled trajectories (GRAM, EBR), rollouts (TRMP), or for CRAM, the number of allowed search moves. By sweeping across allowed inference budgets of each method on 10,000 Sudoku-Extreme test puzzles, we can get a simple “scaling law” plot for inference compute, as shown in Fig. 2a. On this plot, CRAM uses between 282×{\times} (against EBR) and 128,000×{\times} (against EqR) fewer FLOPs than the looped models when compared at each baseline’s most accurate setting. CRAM reaches EBR’s top accuracy (99.86%) using 1.9×1091.9\times 10^{9} FLOPs per puzzle vs EBR’s 5.4×10115.4\times 10^{11} FLOPs. At max accuracy, CRAM solves 99.997% of the puzzles with a mean of 2.0×1092.0\times 10^{9} FLOPs per puzzle. Note that CRAM never returns a wrong answer, it only “misses” where a search reaches its budget before any board passes the stopping threshold.

Diverse valid solutions.

N-Queens and graph coloring test whether the same energy finds many different answers. Since both have many solutions per input, we follow GRAM and EBR [3, 11] and report two scores in Table 3: the accuracy of a single answer (out of N=1N=1 or N=20N=20 chains), and a valid-diversity score over 20 samples (Cov@20). CRAM’s learned energy performs competitively to the best looped baselines across all metrics, despite training in seconds. Note that every Cov@20 value here comes from EBR’s evaluator, since GRAM publishes values from a different normalizer.

4.2 Advantages of explicit energy

Compute that adapts to difficulty.

CRAM’s search stops at the first board whose energy is at most the threshold fitted from the training solutions, which lets CRAM dynamically adjust its compute to follow problem difficulty. When we bin the 10,000 test puzzles of Fig. 2a by the difficulty rating of the dataset (Fig. 3a), the median compute of CRAM grows 22×{\times} from the easiest bin to the hardest. In contrast, FRM spends the same compute for every puzzle and EBR, whose gradient-norm stopping rule enables early stopping for Sudoku, barely changes compute needs across puzzle difficulty. Note that the stopping test of CRAM is also reliable: it never stops at an incorrect board, whereas the halting rules of HRM, TRM, EqR, TRMP and EBR each stop at an incorrect board on 0.05–3.54% of the puzzles that they stop on (Table 4).

Inspectable learned weights.

The nature of these logic puzzles mean we can read the rules of the puzzle directly from CRAM’s learned weights (Fig. 2b). Despite receiving no task-informed constraints for Sudoku, in every training run CRAM learned to put positive equal-digit costs on exactly the 810 cell pairs that share a row, column or box, leaving all other costs zero. On Maze-Unique, the 18 learned costs make each move of the search turn off one dead-end cell, which is dead-end filling [50], a local rule that solves every perfect maze (Sec. C.4).

4.3 Training the energy

Characterizing fast training objectives.

All results above use pseudolikelihood (PL), but the energy of Eq. 1 accepts many other training methods. We compare three classes of training methods on Sudoku-Extreme to see which methods train CRAM the fastest (wall-clock time on a single H200). Local objectives such as PL are evaluated directly at the labeled solution, with no unrolled trajectory during training. Sampling-based methods draw the negative samples of Eq. 4 by unrolling the model, but no differentiation is taken through those unrolled trajectories. A third class differentiates through the relaxation of Eq. 2. This is how looped models are traditionally trained, using truncated or full BPTT, but it also includes methods that approximate BPTT such as implicit differentiation [48, 4]. Fig. 4 shows that local objectives like pseudolikelihood and min probability flow [56] train fastest, followed by short, truncated BPTT. Contrastive divergence follows, and full BPTT (training through all 10 unrolled relaxation steps) fails to solve more than 48.8% after 5 h of training. Full comparison of results are in Table 7 of App. D.

Data efficient learning.

CRAM is data efficient. Fig. 3b explores how many unique Sudoku-Extreme training puzzles are needed to solve a 10k Sudoku-Extreme test set. Each method is provided the same unique puzzles, symmetrically augmented an additional 99 times. On this dataset, CRAM needs an order of magnitude fewer puzzles to reach 98% accuracy than looped models, using only 30 unique puzzles to EBR’s 700. Interestingly, TRM solves the most test puzzles in the extremely data-limited regime (<10<10 puzzles), but it scales much slower than both energy-based methods. In the low-data regime, CRAM converged to many incorrect solutions.

Hand-set energies perform best.

In Tables 2 and 3, we compare a CRAM energy whose weights were set by hand using the rules of a task (Sec. C.7). Under the same search as learned CRAM, the hand-set energies solve every Sudoku, Maze, N-Queens, and Graph Coloring test puzzle, using up to 19×{\times} fewer inference FLOPs than a learned energy on Sudoku. On both N-Queens and Graph Coloring, hand-set CRAM is the top performing model across all metrics and board sizes. A high score on these benchmarks therefore only shows that a model has learned a few pairwise rules between answer cells—a gentle caution against throwing larger looping models at these reasoning problems.

5 Discussion

Recent work has suggested the looping provides an alternative to chain-of-thought on reasoning tasks. In this work, we have used the formal framework of energies to provide a concrete basis for looped models, in which convergence is guaranteed, computations can adapt to problem difficulty, and BPTT can be avoided. We introduced a specific trainable energy, CRAM, and have shown that it is able to learn a suite of commonly used reasoning benchmarks three orders of magnitude faster than other looped methods.

We note that all results with fit times are wall-clock times on a shared cluster, so they vary with concurrent work on a node. For any model that trains on the order of seconds or minutes, where compilation could meaningfully affect reported training times, we report warm fit times that avoid one-time startup costs, such as kernel loading and compilation (see Sec. C.2). Longer runs report cold-fit times.

The puzzles evaluated in this work—Sudoku-Extreme [62], Maze-Unique [36], and the N-Queens and graph-coloring sets of Baek et al. [3]—belong to a category of logic puzzles that CRAM’s pairwise energy can represent exactly [35, 34]. In fact, Table 2 shows that a hand-set CRAM energy with one unique weight value solves every Sudoku-Extreme test puzzle, and one with three values solves every Maze-Unique test maze. High accuracy on these logic benchmarks therefore does not indicate that a model can scale to harder tasks such as ARC-AGI-1 [62, 12], where the answer depends on quantities that the model must compute from the visible board, such as each cell’s distance to the goal in Maze-Hard. In App. F, we show how a simple latent extension of CRAM can learn nearly all of the 1,000 Maze-Hard test mazes, but learning such latent quantities in general and without foreknowledge of the task’s design remains an important open research direction to scale these energies to harder reasoning tasks.

Building efficient reasoning models that are applicable to general tasks is a central challenge in AI research. Our results indicate that energy is a powerful framework for reasoning on constraint puzzles, offering almost 300×{\times} faster inference and 1,000×{\times} faster training than looped models with no loss in accuracy. Though the energy studied here is not a final answer for all reasoning tasks, it showcases the incredible benefit that an explicit energy provides, and provides a promising path towards data-efficient general reasoning capabilities.

Appendix A Stopping rules of looped models and CRAM

HRM, TRM, EqR and TRMP learn early stopping with a separate network [62, 38, 36, 28]. EBR stops a sample when the norm of its energy gradient falls below 0.2 [11]. CRAM is different, stopping at the first board whose energy is at most a threshold fitted from the training solutions. Table 4 shows that only CRAM never stops at an incorrect board — all other early stopping methods do. Note that EBR’s stop does not work on Maze-Unique since its gradient norm stays near 2 even at correct mazes. EBR’s published maze protocol runs a fixed number of segments instead.

Appendix B Compute

Every experiment in this paper runs on one NVIDIA H200 GPU. Training jobs used GPUs on unreserved nodes of a shared cluster, so other jobs could use a node’s other GPUs and CPU cores which could affect reproducibility of timing a fit. Wherever CPU times are reported, they use one thread of an Intel Xeon Platinum 8468 CPU. CRAM’s search moves run in Triton kernels with one GPU warp per chain. A move changes one cell, so the kernel keeps the field of every cell in memory and updates only the fields of the cells with a nonzero coupling to the moved cell. The code, data preparation, run records and exported results behind every table and figure are at https://github.com/Prefrontal-AI/CRAM.

Appendix C Experimental protocols

C.1 Shared protocol

Every method, CRAM and each baseline, is trained three times under different seeds, and each trained model is scored once on the test set. Where a published accuracy was selected on the test set, we say so. The test sets have 412,786 puzzles (Sudoku-Extreme), 1,000 mazes (Maze-Unique), 1,240 and 18,466 rows (N-Queens, 8×88\times 8 and 10×1010\times 10) and 255 and 192 graphs (graph coloring, 8 and 10 vertices).

When reproducing baselines, whenever our three-seed mean accuracy is more 2 points below their published accuracy, a table shows the published value (dagger), but we still count that baseline’s parameters and FLOPs ourselves. A baseline’s Params is the parameter count of its network: we do not check its weights for zeros, so it is an upper bound on the nonzero parameters that CRAM’s count reports.

CRAM inference is a focused Gibbs search with four chains (Sudoku-Extreme) or with NN chains (N=1N{=}1 or 20 in Table 3; N-Queens and graph coloring), and zero-temperature single-cell moves (Maze-Unique). In general, we use each baseline’s published inference setting when solving a task.

  • •

    TRMP: the most confident of 64 noisy rollouts (the ACT model in Table 2).

  • •

    TRMP’s lattice model (the § footnote of Table 2): 64 search chains, each restarted on a detected conflict, for at most 1,000 steps.

  • •

    EqR: depth 64 with 128 noisy restarts, answer chosen by the model’s convergence score [36].

  • •

    GRAM: majority vote of 20 sampled trajectories of 16 steps.

  • •

    EBR: the lowest-energy of five samples; OR when its energy-gradient norm falls below 0.2, or after 64 segments (Sudoku Extreme); OR after 16 updates (Maze-Unique)

C.2 Operation counts and fit time

Reported FLOPs count the operations along all their sampling trajectories, stopping tests, selection amongst samples, and decoding; it excludes losses and metrics computed from labels.

Every FLOP count in this paper, for CRAM and every baseline, uses the following convention:

  • •

    A matrix product counts 2 FLOPs per multiply-add.

  • •

    Every elementwise addition, subtraction, multiplication (also by a 0/1 mask), division, negation and absolute value counts 1, on floats or integers.

  • •

    Every exp, log, square root, sigmoid, tanh and erf counts 1.

  • •

    Comparisons, selections, min, max, argmax, mask logic, indexing, data movement, casts and random-number generation count 0. Arithmetic applied to a random number (scaling noise, a Gumbel transform) counts.

For the neural baselines, a PyTorch counter at the operator-dispatch level applies these rules to every operator during inference, including gradient computations. CRAM’s moves use Triton kernels that are invisible to the counter, so count their transcription line by line. CRAM’s code outside the kernels is counted directly. A CRAM search counts FLOPs up until a move first passes its stopping test.

Reported fit times are the wall clock of one complete fit. The clock starts when the training data are in host memory and stops when the inference-ready model is read, including its stopping statistics. In total, it includes: transfer to the device, initialization, augmentation, every forward, backward and optimizer step, compilation and CUDA-graph capture with their warm-up, and fitting stopping thresholds and focus statistics from the training solutions. It excludes reading files, evaluation, saving and module imports.

We report the warm time for CRAM, because its one-time start-up (0.2–0.9 s on one H200) is a large part of a fit that takes milliseconds, but a negligible part of a baseline fit that takes hours.

  • •

    Cold: the first fit in a fresh process, including one-time kernel loading, compilation and graph capture. CUDA context creation (0.4–0.7 s) is measured separately and excluded.

  • •

    Warm: the median of seven further fits in the same process.

It was not within our compute budget to compute warm-starts for long baseline runs. Thus, each baseline time is one cold fit on one H200 with an empty compilation cache. Its start-up (compilation, kernel loading and the first update) takes 6 s to 16 min, at most 2.2% of the fit (3.5% for TRMP on Maze-Unique).

C.3 CRAM recipes

Table 5 lists the training and search settings of every CRAM fit. Two fits add a step that the table does not list. The Sudoku-Extreme fit applies a fresh random digit relabeling to the training boards at each update. The N-Queens fit divides the gradient of each offset cost by a per-offset preconditioner (Sec. C.5).

C.3.1 Sudoku-Extreme

Sudoku-Extreme [62] (sapientinc/sudoku-extreme) has an official training split and a test split of 422,786 puzzles. CRAM trains on the three 1,000-puzzle training splits of FRM [29], one per seed, which FRM draws from the training split balanced over its difficulty-rating bins. Our development set is 10,000 puzzles of the test split, and our test set is the other 412,786. The cells are opaque indices: CRAM is told neither the rows, columns and boxes nor any structure of the digits. Each pair of cells has a free 9×99\times 9 cost block 𝑲i​j=𝑲j​i⊤\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}K}}_{ij}=\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}K}}_{ji}^{\top} and each cell a free input cost 𝑩i∈ℝ9\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}B}}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{9} (263,169 parameters), clue cells are clamped, and training follows Table 5.

FRM, EqR and TRMP train on the same splits. HRM, TRM, GRAM and EBR keep the data pipeline of their own code: HRM, TRM and GRAM train on one 1,000-puzzle draw from TRM’s data builder (the command of the authors’ README, which fixes no random seed), with 1,000 stored symmetry variants per puzzle, and EBR trains on its own draw (seed 42). Fig. 3b trains CRAM, TRM, EBR and FRM on identical rows.

For CRAM each sudoku puzzle runs four chains from random boards. A move picks a uniformly random free cell whose local energy exceeds its training-solution mean by more than 0.45​h¯0.45\bar{h} (any free cell if there is none) and samples its digit from its belief. The temperature falls geometrically from 0.40​h¯0.40\bar{h} to 0.31​h¯0.31\bar{h} over 524,288 moves and then restarts, and the cached fields are recomputed exactly every 4,096 moves. A puzzle stops at the first board of any chain with energy at most τ+10−3\tau+10^{-3}, where τ\tau is the highest energy of a training solution of its split (−1.7×10−4-1.7\times 10^{-4} to −3×10−6-3\times 10^{-6}), and otherwise returns its lowest-energy board at the budget. We tuned the temperatures and the stopping threshold on development puzzles. On the test set, no search stopped at an incorrect board. 51 of 1,238,358 searches reached the budget.

C.4 Maze-Unique

Maze-Unique [36] (locuslab/EqR-data, subset maze-30x30-unique-1k) has 1,000 training and 1,000 test mazes of 30×3030\times 30 cells, whose answers are a unique path from start to goal. Walls are clamped off, the start and goal on, and PL of the binary path labels is applied at every open cell. We chose the number of updates and the learning rate on 100 held-out training mazes: the fewest updates (10, 20, 50 or 100), then the smallest rate (0.3, 1 or 3), at which every run solves at least 99 of them with focused Gibbs search when trained on nested subsets of 10 to 900 mazes. The final fits use all 1,000 mazes.

Searching a maze starts with every open cell on. Each move sets a uniformly random cell that is not at its lowest-energy value to that value, and the search stops at a fixed point (at most 290 moves were used). From this start, each move turns off one dead-end cell, so the search performs dead-end filling. This choice of start matters since the empty board has lower energy than the solution on every development maze, and explains why exact solvers like toulbar2 can’t find this solution.

C.5 N-Queens

N-Queens uses GRAM’s data [3] without augmentation. An input is a solution with kk queens removed (k∈{5,6,7}k\in\{5,6,7\} on 8×88\times 8, {7,8,9}\{7,8,9\} on 10×1010\times 10), and an input with SS solutions occurs SS times, once with each solution as its label (7,224 training and 1,240 test rows on 8×88\times 8; 108,234 and 18,466 on 10×1010\times 10). Accuracy counts the test rows whose answer is a valid board that keeps every given queen. Cov@20 sums, over distinct test inputs, the distinct valid solutions among 20 samples, capped at min⁡(S,20)\min(S,20), and divides by the sum of min⁡(S,20)\min(S,20). This is the rule of EBR’s evaluator, not GRAM’s. Training follows Table 5, with the gradient of each JdJ_{d} divided by md/m¯m_{d}/\bar{m}, where mdm_{d} is the number of cell pairs at offset dd and m¯\bar{m} its mean. Without this preconditioner, the long diagonals (2 pairs, against 162 for the shortest) barely train since there is insufficient data to learn long correlations.

Each chain starts from the given queens. A move picks a uniformly random free cell whose current state has the higher field (any free cell if there is none) and draws its state with probability proportional to exp(−gi(a)/u)\exp(-g_{i}(a)/u). A chain stops when every free cell has a margin of at least δ−10−3\delta-10^{-3}, or after 20,000 moves with its lowest-energy board; N=1N{=}1 is the first chain, and N=20N{=}20 the lowest-energy board of 20 chains. A rule fixed before testing chose this recipe on 10×1010\times 10 validation inputs; we report it at both sizes, a choice made after seeing the test results (on 8×88\times 8, the rule’s own choice scores 100.00% and 98.3% Cov@20, against 99.95% and 97.9%). To save GPU kernels, the fit builds the pair-cost matrix from the offset costs as one product with a fixed 0/1 matrix instead of by indexing. We timed this fit and tested the models of an indexing fit, whose parameters agree with it to within 10−710^{-7} of the largest parameter.

C.6 Graph coloring

Graph coloring uses GRAM’s graphs with chromatic number 3, each labeled with one 3-coloring in canonical order. We score each graph once. Conflict counts the edges whose two vertices share a color, summed over the test graphs. Cov@20 is the number of distinct proper colorings in canonical order that 20 samples find, over the number of such colorings, summed over graphs (GRAM’s definition). For each pair of vertices, the 3×33\times 3 cost table is an affine function of all the adjacency tokens of the graph, so CRAM is not told which edge belongs to which pair (7,332 and 18,660 parameters; 869 and 475 are nonzero after training). Training follows Table 5.

Each chain starts from a uniformly random coloring and makes the focused moves of Sudoku-Extreme, with focus threshold 0.45​h¯0.45\bar{h}. It stops at the first coloring on which every pair term and input cost is at most its highest value on a training coloring.

C.7 Hand-set energies

Tables 2 and 3 include CRAM energies whose weights we set by hand from the rules of each task (Fig. 5). Reported numbers use the same search as the learned energy on the task.

C.8 Looped-model baselines

We retrain every baseline on one H200 with its authors’ code and recipe: HRM [62] (commit ac15626), TRM [38] (c011037), FRM [29] (6149a01), EqR [36] (134c754), GRAM [3] (f2e32b9) and EBR [11] (8c5271c). The training code of TRMP [52] is not released, so we reimplement two of its recipes: the adaptive computation time (ACT) model of its Appendix B and Table 9 (row TRMP), its most accurate on Sudoku-Extreme, and the 16k-parameter factor-graph lattice model of its abstract (its Table 4), which the § footnote of Table 2 reports. The lattice model trains for 20,000 updates of a 512-board pool, as in that table, and its fit time in the footnote is the median of seven complete fits that follow a first fit in the same process, as for CRAM; the first fit takes 14m46s. GRAM’s paper reports TRM and HRM on N-Queens and graph coloring without a recipe, so we train both in GRAM’s code, which contains both architectures, with GRAM’s per-task settings. Every baseline trains in bf16 with torch.compile, and is scored at its final weights (their exponential moving average where the authors use one), or at a checkpoint chosen on development data (HRM, FRM and TRMP). CRAM fits, in contrast, run as eager PyTorch in single precision, without compilation or CUDA graphs. We change a recipe only where our tests require it:

  • •

    Maze-Unique recipes. HRM, TRM, GRAM and EBR publish no Maze-Unique basline, so we run their Maze-Hard recipes unchanged. GRAM runs the TRM recipe with GRAM’s settings for its non-Sudoku tasks, at global batch 384 (the largest that fits on one H200).

  • •

    Compilation and optimizer. We compile the whole model where the authors’ code does not (FRM; EqR on Maze-Unique), which makes training 1.8–2.2 times faster. TRM and EqR use a pure-PyTorch AdamATan2 in place of the authors’ CUDA package, which adds less than 1% to an update. TRMP trains in bf16, where its paper uses single precision for the Sudoku model.

  • •

    Schedules. HRM trains on Sudoku-Extreme for 40,000 epochs, the schedule of its released checkpoint (though its README states 20,000).

  • •

    Test subset. At 128 restarts, EqR is scored on the first 10,000 Sudoku-Extreme test puzzles, because the full set would take about 105 GPU-hours per seed.

  • •

    Published accuracies. Our GRAM runs solve 93.61 ±\pm 1.21% of Sudoku-Extreme, 2.5 points below the published 96.1%, so Table 2 shows the published value. On Maze-Unique, EqR’s repository configuration (hidden size 44) solves 100.0%, 99.6% and 0% with three seeds, so Table 2 shows the published 93.0% with the parameters, FLOPs and fit time of the paper’s configuration (hidden size 128). On 10×1010\times 10 N-Queens, our TRM and HRM runs solve 6.90% and 22.72%, against the published 17.5% and 37.8%, so Table 3 shows the published values.

C.9 Data efficiency

In Fig. 3b, CRAM, TRM, EBR and FRM train on the same data samples and only the number kk of unique training puzzles changes.

  • •

    Puzzles. For k<1,000k<1{,}000, seed ss takes the first kk puzzles of a seed-ss permutation of TRM’s 1,000-puzzle draw, so the subsets of one seed are nested. k=1,000k=1{,}000 is the whole draw, and k=3,000k=3{,}000 to 100,000 add puzzles from the official training split with the same builder.

  • •

    Augmentation. Each puzzle is augmented with 99 symmetry variants (digit relabeling, transposition, and permutations of bands, stacks, rows and columns). No method adds its own augmentation.

  • •

    CRAM: Training is deterministic, so at k=1,000k=1{,}000 the six seeds give one model and differ only in the search.

  • •

    TRM: 65,100 updates of batch 768 at every kk (65,117 at k=30,000k=30{,}000).

  • •

    EBR: 60,000 updates of batch 768, scored as in Table 2. Its loader needs at least 768 puzzle groups, so for k<768k<768 each group is repeated ⌈768/k⌉\lceil 768/k\rceil times.

  • •

    FRM: Stage A and Stage B of 100,000 updates each at batch 128, checkpoint chosen on 256 development puzzles.

  • •

    Scoring: six runs (seeds 0–5) per point, on the 10,000 test puzzles of Fig. 2a.

Appendix D Training methods for CRAM

As discussed in the paper, there are many ways to train the energy using approximate likelihood methods as per Eq. 4. Table 7 compares twelve such methods across three classes (Table 6). This section describes pseudolikelihood [8] and characterizes the twelve methods on Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique.

D.1 Pseudolikelihood, maximum likelihood, and cross-entropy

Pseudolikelihood (PL) replaces the model term of Eq. 4 with a comparison between the observed solution 𝒙{\color[rgb]{0.0938,0.6406,0.4453}\boldsymbol{x}} and its single-cell changes. Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the cells whose answers the input does not give, and let 𝒙i←a−{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{x}}^{-}_{i\leftarrow a} be 𝒙{\color[rgb]{0.0938,0.6406,0.4453}\boldsymbol{x}} with cell ii set to value aa. We minimize

𝒥PL​(𝜽,𝒙)=E𝜽​(𝒙)⏟   lower energy  on data  +1|ℱ|∑i∈ℱlog∑aexp[−E𝜽(𝒙−i←a)]⏟raise energy on model “samples”,\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{PL}}(\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}};{\color[rgb]{0.0938,0.6406,0.4453}\boldsymbol{x}})=\underbrace{E_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}({\color[rgb]{0.0938,0.6406,0.4453}\boldsymbol{x}})}_{\mathclap{\text{\scriptsize\shortstack{lower energy\\ on data}}}}+\underbrace{\frac{1}{|\mathcal{F}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{F}}\log\sum_{a}\exp\!\left[-E_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{x}}^{-}_{i\leftarrow a})\right]}_{\mathclap{\text{\scriptsize raise energy on model ``samples''}}}, (5)

where aa runs over all permitted values, the labeled one included. Where a task needs it, we add local terms that depend only on the weights and the labeled solution, such as an L1 penalty on the costs. The L1 penalty sets a cost exactly to zero where the examples show no constraint between two cells, so the fitted energy is sparse. Below, we write 𝒚{\color[rgb]{0.0938,0.6406,0.4453}\boldsymbol{y}} for 𝒙{\color[rgb]{0.0938,0.6406,0.4453}\boldsymbol{x}} and 𝒚i←a{\color[rgb]{0.0938,0.6406,0.4453}\boldsymbol{y}}^{i\leftarrow a} for 𝒙i←a−{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{x}}^{-}_{i\leftarrow a}.

At unit temperature, the energy defines a joint distribution P𝜽​(𝒑∣𝒙)=exp⁡[−E𝜽​(𝒑)]/Z𝜽​(𝒙)P_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}\mid{\color[rgb]{0.2891,0.2266,0.6563}\boldsymbol{x}})=\exp[-E_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}})]/Z_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}({\color[rgb]{0.2891,0.2266,0.6563}\boldsymbol{x}}) over the set 𝒮⁡(𝒙)\mathcal{S}({\color[rgb]{0.2891,0.2266,0.6563}\boldsymbol{x}}) of one-hot answer arrays that respect the givens, and maximum likelihood minimizes −log⁡P𝜽​(𝒚∣𝒙)=E𝜽​(𝒚)+log⁡Z𝜽​(𝒙)-\log P_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}({\color[rgb]{0.0938,0.6406,0.4453}\boldsymbol{y}}\mid{\color[rgb]{0.2891,0.2266,0.6563}\boldsymbol{x}})=E_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}({\color[rgb]{0.0938,0.6406,0.4453}\boldsymbol{y}})+\log Z_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}({\color[rgb]{0.2891,0.2266,0.6563}\boldsymbol{x}}) [1, 42]. The partition function Z𝜽​(𝒙)=∑𝒑′∈𝒮⁡(𝒙)exp⁡[−E𝜽​(𝒑′)]Z_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}({\color[rgb]{0.2891,0.2266,0.6563}\boldsymbol{x}})=\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}({\color[rgb]{0.2891,0.2266,0.6563}\boldsymbol{x}})}\exp[-E_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}^{\prime})] sums over up to C|ℱ|C^{|\mathcal{F}|} assignments, so this objective is intractable for the tasks of this paper.

Conditioning on every labeled cell except ii cancels the partition function. With 𝒆a\boldsymbol{e}_{a} the one-hot vector of value aa, the exact conditional of cell ii is a softmax,

qi​(a)≡P𝜽​(𝒑i=𝒆a∣𝒑−i=𝒚−i,𝒙)=exp⁡zi​a∑bexp⁡zi​b,zi​a=−E𝜽​(𝒚i←a),q_{i}(a)\equiv P_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{i}=\boldsymbol{e}_{a}\mid{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{-i}={\color[rgb]{0.0938,0.6406,0.4453}\boldsymbol{y}}_{-i},{\color[rgb]{0.2891,0.2266,0.6563}\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{\exp z_{ia}}{\sum_{b}\exp z_{ib}},\qquad z_{ia}=-E_{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\theta}}}({\color[rgb]{0.0938,0.6406,0.4453}\boldsymbol{y}}^{i\leftarrow a}), (6)

over the permitted values. Eq. 5 is the mean over free cells of the cross-entropy ℓi=−∑ayi​alogqi(a)\ell_{i}=-\sum_{a}{\color[rgb]{0.0938,0.6406,0.4453}y}_{ia}\log q_{i}(a) of the label 𝒚i=(yi​a)a{\color[rgb]{0.0938,0.6406,0.4453}\boldsymbol{y}}_{i}=({\color[rgb]{0.0938,0.6406,0.4453}y}_{ia})_{a}, with the familiar gradient ∂ℓi/∂zi​a=qi​(a)−yi​a\partial\ell_{i}/\partial z_{ia}=q_{i}(a)-{\color[rgb]{0.0938,0.6406,0.4453}y}_{ia}. Every energy term without cell ii cancels in qiq_{i}, so the logits need only the pair and input costs of cell ii, and no inference. Each conditional is exact; the approximation is replacing the joint likelihood with a sum of conditionals [8, 37].

D.2 Comparing twelve objectives

Table 6 lists different training objectives and how it relates to Eq. 4. A relaxation runs nn Euler steps of Eq. 2 (step size 0.5) from uniform beliefs, with clues clamped. Each sampling method lowers the energy of the labeled solution and raises the energy of a negative, a board or belief state drawn from the model; no gradient flows through the drawing of the negative. To keep the energies bounded, each also penalizes their squares, as in Du and Mordatch [19].

A few choices are specific to CRAM. Masked pseudolikelihood sets a hidden cell’s state to zero, so that it adds nothing to the other cells’ fields. Denoising score matching uses the clean logits 3​(𝒚i−𝟏/C)3({\color[rgb]{0.0938,0.6406,0.4453}\boldsymbol{y}}_{i}-\mathbf{1}/C). Contrastive divergence draws its moves at temperature 1, and persistent CD relabels each stored Sudoku chain together with its puzzle. Equilibrium propagation uses β=0.01\beta=0.01, at which its gradient has cosine similarity 0.99999 with the full-BPTT gradient (β=0.5\beta=0.5 diverged). Implicit differentiation runs nn forward and nn adjoint iterations, without a convergence test, and full BPTT uses T=10T=10, selected on both tasks.

Every method trains the energy of Table 2 from the same weight initialization, with SGD (momentum 0.5, cosine schedule) and the L1 penalty as a soft-threshold of ηk​λ\eta_{k}\lambda after each step. All twelve methods run in one shared training harness, so their times compare with each other but not with the fit times of Table 2. The harness is slower than Table 2 because it synchronizes the GPU before and after every update, to time each update and place the development probes.

Each method tunes on seed 0, using development puzzles not in the train or test set:

  • •

    the learning rate: 6, 60 or 540 (Sudoku-Extreme); 0.1, 0.3 or 1 (Maze-Unique);

  • •

    the L1 strength: 1, 0.1 or 0.01 times that of Table 2 (Sudoku-Extreme); 0, 0.003 or 0.03 (Maze-Unique);

  • •

    its own setting: q∈{0.1,0.3}q\in\{0.1,0.3\} (masked PL); σ∈{0.5,1.5}\sigma\in\{0.5,1.5\} (DSM); k∈{81,324}k\in\{81,324\} moves on Sudoku-Extreme and {256,1024}\{256,1024\} on Maze-Unique (CD, persistent CD); n∈{10,30}n\in\{10,30\} on Sudoku-Extreme and {30,100}\{30,100\} on Maze-Unique (contrastive Hebbian learning, equilibrium propagation, implicit differentiation); T∈{10,30}T\in\{10,30\} (truncated and full BPTT); and the weight of the Du and Mordatch [19] regularizer, 0 or 1 (class S).

Pseudolikelihood keeps the learning rate and number of updates of Table 2 and tunes only its L1 strength; every other method runs 2,000 updates (1,500 for class S on Maze-Unique). The rule takes the highest development solve rate, then the shortest fit time. The settings selected for each method are in the code release.

Fig. 4 trains each of its five methods 20 times; its x-axis is the fit time without the one-time start-up, and full BPTT runs 60,000 updates. Four differentiating methods were still improving after 2,000 updates on Sudoku-Extreme, so we gave them longer schedules (footnote of Table 7). Full BPTT, equilibrium propagation and implicit differentiation stop at incorrect boards and fail to train. On Maze-Unique, every method solves every test maze.

Notes on Table 7:

  • •

    T99 is the median over the three runs of the fit time at the first probe where their mean reaches 99%, minus each run’s one-time start-up (0.10–1.83 s on Sudoku-Extreme and 0.64–1.22 s on Maze-Unique), plus the time to fit the stopping threshold and focus statistic (24–75 ms on Sudoku-Extreme; the Maze-Unique search fits none).

  • •

    Contrastive divergence runs 324 heat-bath moves per update on Sudoku-Extreme and 256 on Maze-Unique.

  • •

    The pseudolikelihood row is the recipe of Table 2 under this protocol. Its test solve rates equal those of Table 2, but its fit times and FLOPs differ: it tests the checkpoint chosen on the probe (updates 16, 23 and 16 of 32 on Sudoku-Extreme; 6 of 20 on Maze-Unique), tunes the L1 strength (Maze-Unique selects 0.003, where Table 2 uses none), trains Maze-Unique on 900 mazes, and tests Sudoku-Extreme on 50,000 puzzles.

Appendix E Energy descent

Here we show how deterministic dynamics of Eq. 2 never increase the energy. Define the convex logsumexp function as ℒ⁡(𝒗i)=β−1​log​∑aexp⁡(β​vi​a)\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i})=\beta^{-1}\log\sum_{a}\exp(\beta{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}v}_{ia}). Its derivative is the softmax belief, 𝒑i=∂ℒ/∂𝒗i{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{i}=\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i}, and

𝒗i⊤​𝒑i−ℒ⁡(𝒗i)=β−1​∑api​a​log⁡pi​a.{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i}^{\top}{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{i}-\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i})=\beta^{-1}\sum_{a}{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}p}_{ia}\log{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}p}_{ia}. (7)

so the negative-entropy term of Eq. 1 is the Legendre transform of ℒ\mathcal{L}. For masked cells, all sums and derivatives run over permitted values only. Inside the simplex, the derivative of the energy with respect to a belief is

∂E∂𝒑i=β−1​(log⁡𝒑i+1)+∑j𝑾i​j​𝒑j+𝑩i=𝒗i+∑j𝑾i​j​𝒑j+𝑩i+ci,\frac{\partial E}{\partial{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{i}}=\beta^{-1}(\log{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{i}+1)+\sum_{j}\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}W}}_{ij}{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{j}+\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}B}}_{i}={\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i}+\sum_{j}\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}W}}_{ij}{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{j}+\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}B}}_{i}+c_{i}, (8)

where the scalar ci=β−1−ℒ⁡(𝒗i)c_{i}=\beta^{-1}-\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i}) is added to every entry. So Eq. 2 follows −∂E/∂𝒑i-\partial E/\partial{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{i} up to a constant across values, which leaves the softmax beliefs unchanged. ℒ\mathcal{L} is a convex function, so its Hessian is positive semidefinite:

Hi=∂2ℒ∂𝒗i​∂𝒗i⊤=β⁡[diag⁡(𝒑i)−𝒑i​𝒑i⊤]⪰0.H_{i}=\frac{\partial^{2}\mathcal{L}}{\partial{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i}\,\partial{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i}^{\top}}=\beta\big[\operatorname{diag}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{i})-{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{i}{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{i}^{\top}\big]\succeq 0. (9)

which is singular along the all-ones direction, because adding a constant to all logits leaves the softmax unchanged. Since ∂𝒑i/∂𝒗i=Hi\partial{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{i}/\partial{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i}=H_{i}, and HiH_{i} removes the constant cic_{i}, the chain rule and Eq. 2 give

d​Ed​t=∑i∈ℱ(∂E∂𝒑i)⊤∂𝒑i∂𝒗id​𝒗id​t=−∑i∈ℱτi𝒗˙i⊤Hi𝒗˙i≤0.\frac{dE}{dt}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{F}}\Big(\frac{\partial E}{\partial{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{i}}\Big)^{\!\top}\frac{\partial{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{i}}{\partial{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i}}\frac{d{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i}}{dt}=-\sum_{i\in\mathcal{F}}\tau_{i}\dot{{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}}_{i}^{\top}H_{i}\dot{{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}}_{i}\leq 0. (10)

This holds for fixed inputs, parameters, temperature and clamps, positive time constants, and continuous time. It does not show convergence to a unique minimum, rule out saddles, or say that a minimum is a correct solution. Discrete steps and finite precision need their own analysis.

A board is a single-cell local minimum if no permitted single-cell change lowers its energy. If every labeled cell strictly prefers its label given the other labels, the labeled board is such a minimum. A small average pseudolikelihood loss does not guarantee this for every cell, and it does not say which minimum a search reaches from a puzzle. Focused Gibbs search can pass through higher-energy boards, and it can stop at the energy threshold before it reaches a local minimum.

Appendix F Extending CRAM to Maze-Hard

Summary. The Maze-Unique energy, extended with 11 learned parameters and one hidden layer that settles in its own relaxation, solves 99.9% of the Maze-Hard test mazes after less than 30 seconds of training on one GPU.

On Maze-Unique, the learned energy fills dead ends from the all-open board until only the unique solution path is left (Sec. C.4). Maze-Hard mazes, on the other hand, contain loops that break dead-end filling, because the choice between two sides of a loop depends on distances to the goal. With nowhere in Eq. 1 to store these distance calculations, CRAM solves none of the Maze-Hard test mazes.

To solve this, we can add one layer of hidden neurons 𝒛{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{z}} whose state falls by a fixed amount with each step away from the goal, and let the pair costs of Eq. 1 read it. Training is the pseudolikelihood of Eq. 5, as for the other tasks.

Data.

Maze-Hard [62] has 1,000 training and 1,000 test mazes of 30×3030\times 30 cells, with tokens xi∈{wall,open,S,G}{\color[rgb]{0.2891,0.2266,0.6563}x}_{i}\in\{\text{wall},\text{open},\text{S},\text{G}\} for the start S and the goal G. The label marks one shortest path from S to G, the one that breadth-first search finds with the neighbour order down, left, right, up [11]. Every development training maze has at least 512 shortest paths, so this tie-break decides most labels.

The hidden layer.

Each cell is either a wall, empty, the start S or the goal G. A cell is “open” if it is not a wall. Let 𝒩⁡(i)\mathcal{N}(i) be the set of open side neighbours of an open cell ii. Each open cell has one hidden neuron with output zi{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}z}_{i} and the identity activation; zG{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}z}_{\mathrm{G}} is the output of the neuron at G. The hidden energy is

Ez​(𝒛)=∑i[m2​zi2−12​∑j∈𝒩⁡(i)zi​zj]−zG,E_{z}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{z}})=\sum_{i}\Big[\frac{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}m}}{2}{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}z}_{i}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(i)}{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}z}_{i}{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}z}_{j}\Big]-{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}z}_{\mathrm{G}}, (11)

with one learned mass m{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}m}. The maze enters only through which cells are open, in 𝒩⁡(i)\mathcal{N}(i), and through the position of G. The first term pulls every output toward zero, the second rewards neighbouring outputs that are both large, and the third is a unit input to the neuron at G. A cell has at most four neighbors, requiring that m>4{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}m}>4, (enforced by learning log⁡(m−4)\log({\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}m}-4)). In each row of the Hessian ∇𝒛2Ez\nabla^{2}_{{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{z}}}E_{z}, the diagonal entry m{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}m} is larger than the sum of the other entries, which are at most four entries of size 1, so the Hessian is positive definite. EzE_{z} is then strictly convex and has one minimum 𝒛⋆{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{z}}^{\star}, positive on the cells connected to G and zero elsewhere.

The neurons follow the gradient of the energy,

τ​d​zid​t=−∂Ez∂zi={−m​zi+∑j∈𝒩⁡(i)zj+1,i=G,−m​zi+∑j∈𝒩⁡(i)zj,otherwise.\tau\frac{d{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}z}_{i}}{dt}=-\frac{\partial E_{z}}{\partial{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}z}_{i}}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle-{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}m}{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}z}_{i}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(i)}{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}z}_{j}+1,&i=\mathrm{G},\\[14.0pt] \displaystyle-{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}m}{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}z}_{i}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(i)}{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}z}_{j},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (12)

The time constant τ\tau does not affect the fixed point, only the speed of these dynamics. Letting τ=m\tau={\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}m}, an Euler step of size 1 replaces every output, all at once, by the sum of its neighbours’ outputs (plus 1 at G) divided by m{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}m}:

zi←{1m​(∑j∈𝒩⁡(i)zj+1),i=G,1m​∑j∈𝒩⁡(i)zj,otherwise.{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}z}_{i}\leftarrow\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}m}}\Big(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(i)}{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}z}_{j}+1\Big),&i=\mathrm{G},\\[14.0pt] \displaystyle\frac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}m}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(i)}{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}z}_{j},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (13)

So each neuron takes the sum of its neighbours’ outputs, plus the input at G, damped by the factor 1/m1/{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}m}. This update converges to 𝒛⋆{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{z}}^{\star} from any start. Let the error of a neuron be zi−zi⋆{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}z}_{i}-{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}z}^{\star}_{i}. One update makes the error of each neuron equal to the sum of its neighbours’ errors, divided by m{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}m}. A neuron has at most four neighbours, so each update multiplies the largest error by at most 4/m4/{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}m}, which is less than 1. From 𝒛=𝟎{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{z}}=\boldsymbol{0}, a cell at distance dd from G first becomes nonzero after d+1d+1 updates, so the layer settles in about as many updates as the longest distance (at most 152 on the development mazes).

Solving a maze.

A maze is solved with two relaxations, one after the other (Fig. 6). First, the hidden layer settles, where Eq. 13 updates initial state 𝒛=𝟎{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{z}}=\boldsymbol{0} to fixed point. Then, the answers start with every open cell on and follow Eq. 2. The hidden layer is linked to the visible layer via Li​j​(𝒛){\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}L}_{ij}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{z}}) through attention weights αi​j\alpha_{ij} over ℳ⁡(i)=𝒩⁡(i)∪{i}\mathcal{M}(i)=\mathcal{N}(i)\cup\{i\}:

αi​j​(𝒛)\displaystyle\alpha_{ij}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{z}}) =eβj−i​zj∑k∈ℳ⁡(i)eβk−i​zk,Li​j(𝒛)=κj−iαi​j(𝒛)+κi−jαj​i(𝒛).\displaystyle=\frac{e^{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\beta}_{j-i}}\,{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}z}_{j}}{\sum_{k\in\mathcal{M}(i)}e^{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\beta}_{k-i}}\,{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}z}_{k}},\qquad{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}L}_{ij}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{z}})={\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\kappa}_{j-i}\,\alpha_{ij}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{z}})+{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\kappa}_{i-j}\,\alpha_{ji}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{z}}). (14)

Each answer update of Eq. 3 then adds η​∑j∈ℳ⁡(i)Li​j​(𝒛)​pj\eta\sum_{j\in\mathcal{M}(i)}{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}L}_{ij}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{z}})\,{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}p}_{j} to the Maze-Unique update of cell ii, and learnable βδ{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\beta}_{\delta} (one per direct neighbor, and itself) allows the model to learn Maze-Hard’s preference for direction. The answers pi∈[0,1]{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}p}_{i}\in[0,1] have the same Maze-Unique energy as in Sec. C.4, such that their update is:

𝒗i\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i} ←(1−η)​𝒗i−η⁡(∑j(𝑾i​j⏟Maze-Unique−Li​j​(𝒛)​diag⁡(0,1)⏟links to the hidden layer)​𝒑j+𝑩i),\displaystyle\leftarrow(1-\eta)\,{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i}-\eta\Big(\sum_{j}\big(\underbrace{\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}W}}_{ij}}_{\mathclap{\text{\scriptsize Maze-Unique}}}-\underbrace{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}L}_{ij}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{z}})\operatorname{diag}(0,1)}_{\mathclap{\text{\scriptsize links to the hidden layer}}}\big){\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{j}+\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}B}}_{i}\Big), (15)
𝒑i\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{p}}_{i} =softmax⁡(𝒗i).\displaystyle=\operatorname{softmax}({\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i}).

Here 𝒗i∈ℝ2{\color[rgb]{0.1641,0.4688,0.8398}\boldsymbol{v}}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} holds the logits of the off and on states of cell ii, and 𝑾i​j\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}W}}_{ij} and 𝑩i\boldsymbol{{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}B}}_{i} are the 2×22\times 2 pair costs and the input cost of the Maze-Unique energy, so with L=0{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}L}=0 this is Eq. 3 for Maze-Unique; diag⁡(0,1)\operatorname{diag}(0,1) keeps only the on–on entry, so a link lowers the cost of two linked cells being on together. The links raise the on logit of cell ii by the on probabilities of itself and its neighbours, weighted by their links. Walls stay off, and S and G stay on.

The fixed point of this optimization is the predicted path.

Training uses pseudolikelihood training as in Maze-Unique, and an adjoint solver for the hidden parameters, without differentiating through either relaxation. The model has 29 total learned parameters: the 18 of the Maze-Unique energy, five κ{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\kappa}, five β{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\beta} and m{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}m}: with κ=0{\color[rgb]{0.9219,0.4063,0.2031}\kappa}=0 it is the Maze-Unique model.

Results.

On the development mazes, each of three training runs solves 100 of 100. Trained on all 1,000 training mazes and scored once on the test set, each of three runs solves 999 of 1,000, with one incorrect stop and no exhausted budget (Table 8). All three fail on the same maze, where a dead end of six cells along the maze’s border, next to the path, stays on: its cells support each other through the 3×33\times 3 pair costs, so the flow does not prune it. On the development mazes, learning an input per token in place of the input at G solves 0 of 300, and one gate per pair in place of the normalized window weights solves 0 of 100. A fit takes about half a minute on one H200, with the hidden-layer relaxation and its adjoint each run as one fused Triton kernel per maze.
